MAEDIN Goal 4

Engage in lifelong learning for continuous improvement in professional practice and collaborative leadership.

Scroll down to begin

Personal Statement

I work at the Multifunctional Inclusive Resource Center under the National Agency for Social Protection of the Republic of Uzbekistan. In the department for the certification of trainees and teachers, my team develops standards for educators and individual development plans for children with special educational needs. Before this, I taught English.

If one thread runs through everything I do, it is this: I want to help the education system of Uzbekistan change. People who know me usually notice it before I say it aloud. I study constantly, partly for work and partly out of plain curiosity.

For a long time, I believed knowledge mattered more than paper. I still do. Yet building this notebook showed me a gap: much of what I learned left no visible trace. Schön (1983) describes this kind of knowledge precisely: "Often we cannot say what it is that we know" (p. 49). Society, on the other hand, tends to trust what it can see.

This notebook is my attempt to bring those two sides together. I rely on Kolb's (1984) definition of learning as "the process whereby knowledge is created through the transformation of experience" (p. 38). Seen this way, a certificate marks only the end point, while the learning itself happened in between. Niguidula (2019) makes a similar point: a portfolio becomes more than an electronic file cabinet only when it is used for reflection and assessment. Following Gibson et al. (2015), I treat each badge as a visible record of an achievement that should also carry links explaining its context and process. For this reason, every page here ends with evidence.

“Often we cannot say what it is that we know.”

Schön, 1983, p. 49

A note on format. The assignment suggested OneNote or Adobe Express. Since the instructions also invite students to look for more suitable tools, I built this using a different platform, which gave me more freedom in layout and navigation.

How to Read This Notebook

The badges follow my path in time, from 2021 to 2026. This order echoes Dewey's principle of continuity: every experience takes something from earlier ones and shapes the ones that follow (Dewey, 1938, as cited in Kolb, 1984). It also mirrors the "growth over time" tour described by Niguidula (2019), in which learners look back at how they got where they are.

Each badge carries two labels. The first comes from Niguidula (2019): required badges show what the program expects from every student, whereas personal badges show a learner's own interests. The second names the element of Goal 4 that the badge speaks to most clearly.

Every badge page has the same parts: what the badge represents, my reflection, the theory behind it, what it means for my practice, and a link to evidence.

First Steps in Research: "Science and Youth" Conference (2021)

01Research & Inquiry
Issued by
Central Kazakhstan Academy, Karaganda
Date
February 26, 2021

PersonalLifelong learning

What it represents

A first-degree diploma for my paper "The Role of Media Culture in the Formation of Personality," presented at the VII International Scientific-Theoretical Conference of Students and Master's Students "Science and Youth: New Ideas and Solutions." My supervisor was Professor M. I. Israil.

Reflection

My paper explored media culture and the shifts it creates in the way people think. It was my first time presenting research at an international level. Looking back, I value the habit it started more than the diploma itself: asking how culture shapes the way people learn. Schön (1983) argues that a practitioner who reflects in action "becomes a researcher in the practice context" (p. 68). In my current job, I analyze systems and draw conclusions from them almost daily, so that early habit has simply moved from the conference hall into practice.

Looking ahead

Media culture is no longer an abstract topic for me. My team now creates infographics and guides with the help of AI, and I keep returning to the same question I asked in 2021: how does what people see shape what they learn?

Badge 2 of 9

Learning Through Dialogue: UNESCO Youth Forum (2021)

02Learning in Dialogue

At the forum, nobody deposited knowledge into anyone; we built it together.

Issued by
International Centre for the Rapprochement of Cultures under the auspices of UNESCO, Almaty
Date
March 16, 2021

PersonalCollaborative leadership

What it represents

A certificate for active participation in the I International Forum for Children's and Youth Initiatives "The Great Silk Road: The Road of Dialogue," on the theme "International Youth Interaction on the Silk Road."

Reflection

Students and schoolchildren gathered to talk about education and about how media is connected to what people learn. We worked as a team, and the conversation moved freely across ages and cultures. Freire describes true dialogue as a joint inquiry among equals and sets it against the "banking" model, in which knowledge is simply deposited into learners (Freire, 1974, as cited in Kolb, 1984). At the forum, nobody deposited knowledge into anyone; we built it together.

Looking ahead

Today, I regularly speak with partners from other countries to set up collaboration in inclusive education. The forum was my first taste of this kind of work. It taught me that cooperation across cultures needs patience before it needs answers.

PersonalLifelong learning

What it represents

Confirmation of a German course at level C1.1, completed "with very good success," and an IELTS Academic result at CEFR level C1.

Reflection

I learn languages mainly because I enjoy them. I have also studied French, although I have no certificate for it. Dewey's principle of continuity fits languages especially well: what a person learns in one situation becomes a tool for the situations that follow (Dewey, 1938, as cited in Kolb, 1984). German, which I once studied for myself, now helps me in communication with German-speaking partners. English, in turn, is part of almost every international call I join, and for several years it was also the subject I taught.

Looking ahead

Niguidula (2019) warns that reflections built around scores rarely lead to real insight. For this reason, I see these documents less as results and more as instruments: each language widens the circle of people and sources I can learn from.

Changing a System from Within: Change Academy (2021–2022)

04Leading Change

For the first time, I saw myself as someone who could change an institution rather than simply work inside it.

Issued by
British Council and Advance HE
Date
November 2021 – March 2022

PersonalCollaborative leadership

What it represents

Completion of the Higher Education for Employability, Change Academy Programme, as part of a team from Uzbekistan State World Languages University.

Reflection

A teacher from my university invited me to join the programme, and we went through it together. Our team worked on problems in adult education and looked for ways to change the system from the inside. Honestly, I no longer remember the exact solution we reached. What I do remember is how much I enjoyed the process, and Kolb (1984) would hardly be surprised: in his view, learning is "best conceived as a process, not in terms of outcomes" (p. 26). Schön (1983) adds that practitioners can reflect on "the role he has constructed for himself within a larger institutional context" (p. 62). For the first time, I saw myself as someone who could change an institution rather than simply work inside it.

Looking ahead

My current work on standards for educators is also system change. Change Academy gave me an early model of how it happens: in a team, step by step, with a teacher and a student working as equals.

From student to practitioner

These two documents mark a turn: from studying languages to teaching them, and later to shaping how other teachers work.

The Foundation: Bachelor's Degree with Honours (2023)

06A Strong Foundation
Issued by
Uzbekistan State World Languages University
Date
July 8, 2023

PersonalLifelong learning

What it represents

A bachelor's degree with honours in Linguistics on Intercultural Communication, with the qualification of intercultural communication linguist and translator-referent.

Reflection

My graduation thesis compared different language patterns and grammatical structures and asked which of their features matter most. On paper, it was a linguistic study. In practice, the degree gave me something wider: the ability to read the cultural and political context behind a person's words. Colleagues often trust me with complex communication for this reason, even though I find it hard to explain exactly how I do it. Kolb (1984) notes that a holistic view of learning builds bridges between life situations such as school and work, presenting learning as a continuous, lifelong process (p. 33). My degree is one of those bridges.

Looking ahead

In inclusive education, families, specialists and ministries each speak their own professional "language." Intercultural skills help me translate between them, not only between national languages.

Confirming What I Knew: 120-Hour TESOL/TEFL Certificate (2025)

07Teaching & Practice

When a method does not work for a child, it is the method that has to change.

Issued by
World TESOL Academy
Date
February 23, 2025
Certificate No.
WTA22261065

PersonalContinuous improvement

What it represents

An accredited course on teaching English to non-native speakers in classroom and online settings, accredited by ACCREDITAT and The CPD Certification Service.

Reflection

I already had teaching experience when I took this course. I took it for myself: I wanted international confirmation that my skills were real. From my teaching practice, the approach I rely on most is Socratic questioning. Good questions pull me out of "blank page" moments and point me to things I had not yet considered. Schön (1983) lists similar questions that practitioners ask themselves, such as "How am I framing the problem that I am trying to solve?" (p. 50). In Kolb's (1984) cycle, questions like this move a learner from concrete experience to reflective observation.

Looking ahead

Schön (1983) retells Tolstoy's view that a good teacher treats a pupil's difficulty as a defect of his own instruction, not of the pupil (p. 66). In inclusive education, this idea is central. When a method does not work for a child, it is the method that has to change.

Chapter III Badges 8–9

2026

Practice in the age of AI

The two required badges bring the path to the present, where my work depends on using AI wisely and keeping academic work honest.

2026
08

Badge 8 of 9 (required)

AI Literacy: Microsoft AI Courses (2026)

08Responsible AI
Issued by
Microsoft
Date
October 1, 2026

RequiredContinuous improvement

What it represents

Completion of two Microsoft courses: AI for Educators and Introduction to Generative AI for Trainers.

Reflection

These courses mostly confirmed what I already understood about how AI works, and that confirmation has its own value. I use AI every day: to create images and infographics for our reports and methodological guides, to analyze systems, and to search for literature. When I need books on a topic, I ask AI to find comparable sources, and then I read them myself and draw my own conclusions. The courses also reminded me that specific instructions and clear context are what make an AI output useful.

Responsible AI use belongs to what Schön (1983) calls the "swampy lowland," where situations are "confusing 'messes' incapable of technical solution" (p. 42). No rule tells me when an AI-generated image is accurate enough or when a source it suggests is reliable; I have to judge. Kolb's (1984) reminder that "all learning is relearning" (p. 28) applies here as well, since working with AI means questioning old habits of searching, writing and designing.

Looking ahead

In my department, I want to help teachers use AI in the same way: as a starting point, never as the final word.

Badge 9 of 9 (required)

Academic Integrity: How to Recognize Plagiarism (2026)

09Academic Integrity
Issued by
Indiana University Bloomington, School of Education
Date
October 1, 2026

RequiredContinuous improvement

What it represents

An Advanced Level Certificate for master's and doctoral students. To earn it, I had to answer at least 9 of 10 randomly selected questions correctly, deciding each time whether a student text was word-for-word plagiarism, paraphrasing plagiarism, or not plagiarism.

Reflection

The course was more unusual and harder than I expected. The line between paraphrasing and plagiarism was not always where I thought it would be. Sometimes a text looked like a simple retelling of ideas and turned out to be acceptable; in other cases, the reverse was true. Kolb (1984), drawing on Hegel, observes that an experience which does not violate our expectations hardly deserves the name (p. 28). My expectations were violated several times, and that is precisely where I learned. In Schön's (1983) terms, integrity is another "swamp": it cannot be checked mechanically and requires judgment.

Looking ahead

Academic integrity and AI are now closely linked, since AI tools can paraphrase a text in seconds. As my team creates guides and standards for educators, I want proper citation to become a normal part of that work, and a skill we model for the teachers we certify.

Overall Reflection

Taken together, these nine pages show me three things I had not seen before.

First, the path is not random. Linguistics led to languages, languages led to teaching, teaching led to questions about systems, and those questions brought me to my current work on standards for educators. Dewey's idea of continuity, as presented by Kolb (1984), describes this better than I could: each step became a tool for the next.

Second, experience alone is not enough. Kolb (1984) recalls the saying about a person who has "one year repeated 20 times" instead of twenty years of experience (p. 35). Schön (1983) warns about something similar: when practice turns into routine, a practitioner may end up having "over-learned" what he knows and stop thinking about what he is doing (p. 61). For me, lifelong learning is the opposite of that routine. Every new course, and every reflection like this one, switches off the automatic mode.

Third, the evidence is uneven, and I accept that. Several experiences left almost no documents behind, and some things I studied purely out of interest, such as French, left none at all. Niguidula (2019) tells the story of students who could not remember everything they had done by graduation and asked to update their résumés every year. I recognize myself in them. My conclusion is simple: knowledge still matters more than paper, yet knowledge that nobody can see is hard to share, verify or build on.

Finally, I now look at difficulties differently. They are not a burden I carry but steps I pass through. Kolb (1984) describes learning as a process filled with tension and conflict (p. 30), and building this notebook confirmed it.

Applying This Strategy in My Work

My department certifies trainees and teachers and develops individual development plans for children with special educational needs. In other words, I already work with the question this notebook asks: how can growth be made visible and trustworthy? Niguidula (2019) notes that the badge process he describes for students can equally be applied to badges earned by teachers.

For teachers

I see a clear place for micro-credentials in professional development for inclusive education. A large standard could be divided into smaller badges, each linked to evidence from real practice: a lesson plan, an adapted material or a short case reflection. Following Niguidula (2019), teachers could combine required badges, set by the standard, with personal badges that show their own specialties. The reflection prompts he cites from Mt. Hope High School would fit naturally: What does this skill mean to me? How does my evidence show it? How will it help me in the future?

For children

An individual development plan already focuses on one child rather than on a class average. A simple portfolio of a child's work and achievements could make that plan more visible to families and specialists. As Deborah Meier argues, no child should remain anonymous (Meier, 2002, as cited in Niguidula, 2019).

A note of caution

Badges do not work automatically. Abramovich et al. (2013) found that their effect depends on the type of badge and on the learner's level of expertise. Any system we build would therefore need careful design, regular feedback and, above all, honest reflection instead of collecting for the sake of collecting.

Advice to a New MAEDIN Student

Stay one step ahead of your own curiosity. Even if you already consider yourself a curious person, assume you can go further.

One practical thing, too: start keeping records from your very first week. Save your certificates, slides and drafts, and write a few lines about what each of them taught you. Then, when a task like this one arrives, you will not have to rebuild your path from memory, as I did.

Thank you for reading.

Why curiosity? Because for me it is a way of moving forward that never really ends: every answer opens a new question, and every question leads to something more. Alfred Tennyson put it into one line:

Anastasiya Potapova
